subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal cyst disorders: ADPKD, ARPKD, simple vs complex cysts
vignette: A 36-year-old man with a family history of kidney disease undergoes genetic testing after imaging shows numerous bilateral renal cysts. His father required dialysis in his 50s. Which of the following genetic abnormalities is most likely responsible?
question: Which gene mutation best explains this patient's autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease?

options.text: Mutation in PKHD1 encoding fibrocystin on chromosome 6
Deletion of a gene on chromosome 3 associated with von Hippel-Lindau syndrome
Mutation in a gene on chromosome 4 accounting for 85% of cases
Mutation in PKD1 encoding polycystin on chromosome 16, the most common cause
Mutation in the gene for medullary cystic kidney disease

explanation_correct: ADPKD is caused by mutations in genes encoding polycystin: PKD1 (about 85% of cases, on chromosome 16) and PKD2 (about 15% of cases, on chromosome 4). PKD1 mutations are the most common and tend to cause more severe disease with earlier progression to renal failure, matching this patient's family history of dialysis in the 50s. The cysts occur in both cortex and medulla, producing bilaterally enlarged kidneys. A useful reminder is that PKD1 is on chromosome 16 and is far more common than PKD2 on chromosome 4.

explanation_incorrect.A: PKHD1 encodes fibrocystin and causes autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease, typically presenting in infancy, not adult-onset dominant disease.
explanation_incorrect.B: A chromosome 3 deletion is associated with clear cell renal cell carcinoma and von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, not ADPKD.
explanation_incorrect.C: Chromosome 4 (PKD2) accounts for only about 15% of ADPKD cases, not 85%; PKD1 on chromosome 16 accounts for 85%.
explanation_incorrect.E: Medullary cystic kidney disease (AD tubulointerstitial kidney disease) causes small kidneys with concentrating defects, not the numerous bilateral cysts of ADPKD.

educationalObjective: ADPKD is most often due to PKD1 (polycystin, chromosome 16, 85%); PKD2 (chromosome 4) accounts for 15%.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal cyst disorders: ADPKD, ARPKD, simple vs complex cysts
vignette: A 41-year-old woman with ADPKD has hypertension and flank pain. During evaluation she is found to have a mitral valve abnormality and multiple benign liver cysts. Which of the following additional associations would most likely be found in this patient?
question: Which of the following is a recognized extrarenal association of ADPKD?

options.text: Congenital hepatic fibrosis and Potter sequence
Berry aneurysms and diverticulosis
Cafe-au-lait spots and Lisch nodules
Cardiac rhabdomyomas and ash-leaf spots
Retinal hemangioblastomas and pancreatic cysts

explanation_correct: ADPKD is associated with several extrarenal manifestations, including berry aneurysms (notably of the circle of Willis), mitral valve prolapse, benign hepatic cysts, and diverticulosis. These reflect the widespread role of polycystins in epithelial and vascular tissue. This patient already has mitral valve prolapse and hepatic cysts, and berry aneurysms and diverticulosis are additional classic associations. Rupture of a berry aneurysm is a serious potential complication.

explanation_incorrect.A: Congenital hepatic fibrosis and Potter sequence are associations of autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease (PKHD1), not ADPKD.
explanation_incorrect.C: Cafe-au-lait spots and Lisch nodules are features of neurofibromatosis type 1, not ADPKD.
explanation_incorrect.D: Cardiac rhabdomyomas and ash-leaf spots are features of tuberous sclerosis, not ADPKD.
explanation_incorrect.E: Retinal hemangioblastomas and pancreatic cysts are associations of von Hippel-Lindau syndrome, not ADPKD.

educationalObjective: ADPKD extrarenal associations: berry aneurysms, mitral valve prolapse, benign hepatic cysts, diverticulosis.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal cyst disorders: ADPKD, ARPKD, simple vs complex cysts
vignette: A 39-year-old man with ADPKD presents with worsening flank pain, hematuria, and hypertension (BP 158/96 mm Hg). He has had two urinary tract infections. His creatinine is rising. Which of the following best summarizes his disease and its management?
question: Which statement best describes ADPKD and the appropriate management of his hypertension?

options.text: Bilateral enlarged kidneys with flank pain, hematuria, hypertension, and urinary infection; treat hypertension or proteinuria with ACE inhibitors or ARBs
Small echogenic kidneys with inability to concentrate urine; manage with fluid restriction alone
A solitary unilateral cyst that requires immediate surgical resection
Collecting duct dilation presenting in infancy with congenital hepatic fibrosis
Nephrotic-range proteinuria treated with high-dose corticosteroids

explanation_correct: ADPKD produces numerous cysts in the cortex and medulla, causing bilaterally enlarged kidneys that ultimately destroy renal parenchyma. Patients present with combinations of flank pain, hematuria, hypertension, and urinary infection, with progressive renal failure in about 50% of individuals. Hypertension results in part from increased renin production. When hypertension or proteinuria develops, ACE inhibitors or ARBs are recommended. This patient's presentation and management fit that description.

explanation_incorrect.B: Small echogenic kidneys with impaired urine concentration describe autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial (medullary cystic) kidney disease, not ADPKD's enlarged cystic kidneys.
explanation_incorrect.C: ADPKD is a diffuse bilateral cystic disease, not a solitary unilateral cyst; a simple unilateral cyst would be a different entity.
explanation_incorrect.D: Collecting duct dilation with congenital hepatic fibrosis and infantile presentation describes ARPKD (PKHD1), not adult ADPKD.
explanation_incorrect.E: ADPKD does not typically cause nephrotic-range proteinuria requiring corticosteroids; the proteinuria, when present, is managed with ACEi/ARB.

educationalObjective: ADPKD causes bilateral enlarged kidneys with flank pain, hematuria, HTN, UTI, and progressive failure; ACEi/ARB treat HTN/proteinuria.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal cyst disorders: ADPKD, ARPKD, simple vs complex cysts
vignette: A newborn is found on prenatal ultrasound to have symmetrically enlarged, echogenic kidneys. After birth the infant has oliguric renal failure and respiratory distress due to pulmonary hypoplasia. Examination reveals an enlarged liver with fibrosis. Which of the following best explains this presentation?
question: Which diagnosis and mechanism best account for this newborn's findings?

options.text: ADPKD due to PKD1 mutation with berry aneurysm formation
Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease with concentration defect
Simple renal cysts with incidental hepatic involvement
Clear cell renal cell carcinoma with paraneoplastic syndrome
ARPKD due to PKHD1 mutation causing collecting duct dilation and congenital hepatic fibrosis, with Potter sequence from in utero oliguria

explanation_correct: ARPKD results from mutations in PKHD1 encoding fibrocystin, causing cystic dilation of the collecting ducts. It often presents in infancy and may be detected on prenatal ultrasound as enlarged echogenic kidneys. It is associated with congenital hepatic fibrosis. Significant oliguric renal failure in utero reduces amniotic fluid and leads to Potter sequence (pulmonary hypoplasia, characteristic facies, limb deformities) - explaining this infant's respiratory distress. Beyond the neonatal period, survivors can develop systemic hypertension, progressive renal insufficiency, and portal hypertension from hepatic fibrosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: ADPKD (PKD1) typically presents in adults with enlarged cystic kidneys and berry aneurysms, not a neonate with congenital hepatic fibrosis and Potter sequence.
explanation_incorrect.B: AD tubulointerstitial kidney disease features small kidneys and an inability to concentrate urine with poor prognosis, not neonatal collecting duct dilation and hepatic fibrosis.
explanation_incorrect.C: Simple cysts are anechoic, incidental, and asymptomatic; they do not cause neonatal oliguric failure or congenital hepatic fibrosis.
explanation_incorrect.D: Clear cell RCC is a tumor of adults with chromosome 3/VHL alterations and paraneoplastic syndromes, not a congenital cystic disease of the newborn.

educationalObjective: ARPKD (PKHD1/fibrocystin) causes collecting duct dilation, congenital hepatic fibrosis, and Potter sequence from in utero oliguria.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal cyst disorders: ADPKD, ARPKD, simple vs complex cysts
vignette: A 45-year-old man from a family with autosomal dominant kidney disease has slowly progressive renal insufficiency. He reports producing large volumes of dilute urine and has difficulty concentrating his urine. Ultrasound shows small kidneys without visible cysts. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
question: Which diagnosis best fits this patient's small kidneys, concentrating defect, and progressive renal insufficiency?

options.text: Autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
Autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease
Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease (medullary cystic kidney disease)
Simple renal cysts
Renal papillary necrosis

explanation_correct: Autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease, also called medullary cystic kidney disease, causes tubulointerstitial fibrosis and progressive renal insufficiency with an inability to concentrate urine. The medullary cysts are usually not visualized on imaging, and the kidneys are small on ultrasound - matching this patient's findings. It carries a poor prognosis. The key distinctions from ADPKD are the small rather than enlarged kidneys, the prominent concentrating defect, and the lack of visible cysts.

explanation_incorrect.A: ADPKD causes bilaterally enlarged kidneys with numerous visible cysts, flank pain, hematuria, and hypertension, not small kidneys with a concentrating defect.
explanation_incorrect.B: ARPKD presents in infancy with collecting duct dilation, congenital hepatic fibrosis, and enlarged echogenic kidneys, not adult-onset small kidneys.
explanation_incorrect.D: Simple cysts are anechoic, incidental, and asymptomatic and do not cause progressive renal insufficiency or a concentrating defect.
explanation_incorrect.E: Papillary necrosis causes gross hematuria and sloughed papillae with SAAD associations, not small kidneys with a chronic concentrating defect.

educationalObjective: AD tubulointerstitial (medullary cystic) kidney disease: small kidneys, inability to concentrate urine, non-visible medullary cysts, poor prognosis.

vignette: A 55-year-old man undergoes abdominal CT for unrelated abdominal pain and is found to have a 2-cm fluid-filled renal lesion. It is anechoic on ultrasound, has no septations or solid components, and does not enhance with contrast. He is asymptomatic. Which of the following best characterizes this lesion?
question: Which of the following best describes this renal lesion?

options.text: A complex cyst requiring surgical removal to exclude malignancy
A simple cyst filled with ultrafiltrate, the most common type of renal mass
A clear cell renal cell carcinoma arising from the proximal tubule
A cyst associated with tuberous sclerosis and angiomyolipoma
A medullary cyst from autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease

explanation_correct: Simple renal cysts are filled with ultrafiltrate and are anechoic on ultrasound. They are very common, accounting for the majority of all renal masses, and are typically found incidentally and are asymptomatic. The absence of septations, solid components, or contrast enhancement supports a benign simple cyst, which requires no intervention. This contrasts with complex cysts, which need follow-up or removal.

explanation_incorrect.A: Complex cysts are septated, enhanced, or contain solid components and require follow-up or removal because of RCC risk; this lesion has none of those features.
explanation_incorrect.C: Clear cell RCC is a solid, enhancing, golden-yellow tumor of proximal tubule origin, not a simple anechoic fluid-filled cyst.
explanation_incorrect.D: Cysts in tuberous sclerosis are associated with angiomyolipomas and other features; this isolated simple cyst in an asymptomatic adult is the common benign lesion.
explanation_incorrect.E: Medullary cysts of AD tubulointerstitial kidney disease are usually not visualized and occur with small kidneys and concentrating defects, not an incidental anechoic cyst.

educationalObjective: Simple renal cysts are anechoic ultrafiltrate-filled masses, the most common renal mass, incidental and asymptomatic.

subject: Renal
subtopic: Renal cyst disorders: ADPKD, ARPKD, simple vs complex cysts
vignette: A 64-year-old man has a 4-cm renal lesion found on CT. It contains thin septations, shows internal enhancement after contrast, and has a small solid mural nodule. He has a history of smoking. Which of the following is the most appropriate interpretation and management?
question: How should this renal lesion be interpreted and managed?

options.text: A complex cyst with septations, enhancement, and solid components that requires follow-up or removal to exclude renal cell carcinoma
A simple benign cyst that can be ignored regardless of its appearance
A finding pathognomonic for autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease
A medullary cyst indicating autosomal dominant tubulointerstitial kidney disease
A renal papilla sloughed from papillary necrosis requiring only observation

explanation_correct: Complex renal cysts - those that are septated, enhance with contrast, or contain solid components - raise concern for renal cell carcinoma and require follow-up imaging or surgical removal. This lesion's septations, enhancement, and solid mural nodule are suspicious features, particularly in an older smoker (a demographic with increased RCC incidence). Simple cysts by contrast are anechoic, nonenhancing, and benign. The presence of solid/enhancing components is what mandates further evaluation to exclude malignancy.

explanation_incorrect.B: A lesion with septations, enhancement, and a solid nodule is not a simple cyst and cannot be ignored; complex features require follow-up or removal.
explanation_incorrect.C: ADPKD produces numerous bilateral cysts in enlarged kidneys with a family history, not a single complex septated enhancing lesion.
explanation_incorrect.D: Medullary cysts of AD tubulointerstitial kidney disease are usually not visualized and are associated with small kidneys and concentrating defects, not a complex enhancing mass.
explanation_incorrect.E: Sloughed papillae from papillary necrosis present with hematuria and calyceal filling defects with SAAD associations, not a septated enhancing cyst.

educationalObjective: Complex renal cysts (septated, enhanced, or solid components) require follow-up/removal to exclude RCC; simple cysts are benign.
